Need to search first.I couldn't do as much research as I meant to. The search tool hit its usage limit partway through, and none of the full pages would load. These notes come only from the search-result extracts I could read. That shows in the coverage:

- **Missing sources:** I found nothing from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. All of those are left out.
- **Thin verses:** I found very little on vv. 25–37, and nothing specific on vv. 30, 36 or 47.
- **Names on the Bible Hub pages:** The extracts mix several commentators together, and not every paragraph shows whose it is. I've named a commentator only where the extract labels them. Where it doesn't, I say "unattributed."

---

**Background for the whole passage (useful before v. 25)**
- Guzik (Enduring Word) sets out four ways of reading Ezekiel 40–48: literal fulfilment by the returning exiles, symbolic, dispensationalist (a millennial temple) and apocalyptic. He concludes the temple is "real, yet to be fulfilled" and probably belongs to the millennial age. He quotes another writer saying the church Fathers and Reformers favoured the symbolic (Christ-and-church) reading. He also cites Feinberg: the sheer amount of detail makes a figurative reading hard. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/
- Matthew Henry reads the temple as a picture of the spiritual worship of the gospel age. He says it is "perfected at last in the kingdom of glory." He notes that some put its fulfilment in a glorious latter-day state of the church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_040.cfm
- Precept Austin's index says a literal reading points to the millennial temple, to which Christ's glory returns. It also reports that one critical commentary it reviews calls the future-temple reading "a desperate expedient." https://www.preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_commentaries

---

**vv. 25–27 (south gate of the outer court)**
- Guzik: the south gate had the same measurements as the others. He notes there was no gate on the west, because the temple stood closer to the western wall. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/
- Henry: neither the outer nor the inner court has a gate toward the west. He notes that Solomon's temple seems to have had west gates, since porters were stationed there. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_040.cfm

**vv. 28–37 (the inner-court gates: south, east, north)**
- Henry says the inner gates matched the outer gates exactly. His lesson: grace works the same way in mature Christians as in beginners, "only that the former have got so much nearer their perfection." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_040.cfm
- **vv. 31, 34, 37 (eight steps):** Henry contrasts the seven steps up to the outer court with eight up to the inner. The people rise above the world, and the priests must rise one step higher still: "the nearer we approach to God the more we should rise above this world." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Eze/Eze_040.cfm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/40.htm

**v. 38 (washing room)**
- Ellicott (unattributed in the extract, but it opens the Bible Hub page): the word for "chamber" is different from the one used earlier, so it means "a cell with its door." He notes that all the sacrifice arrangements are described at the north gate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: this applies only to the north gate, because Lev. 1:11 puts the slaughter north of the altar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: there was a washing cell at every inner gate, not only the north one. That fits 46:1–2, where offerings come through the east gate. Only the entrails and legs were washed (Lev. 1:9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: lists the competing views (all three gates, the north only, the east only) and the scholars behind each. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Cambridge (unattributed): this is not the usual word for "wash." The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) thinks of a drain for the blood. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Constable: there was a rinsing room outside each of the three inner gates. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-39.html
- Darby's note: "rinsed" means "thoroughly washed." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsn/ezekiel-40.html
- Gill: these are gospel times, so no legal sacrifice is meant. The washing stands for the spotless purity of Christ's sacrifice. He reports that Polanus saw baptism here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-38.html
- Henry: before we approach God's altar we must wash "our hands, our hearts." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/40.htm
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary quotes Lange: our hearts can stay unclean even in great self-sacrifice. Putting the flesh to death has to rest on Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-39.html

**v. 39 (tables for slaughter)**
- Guzik: these offerings need not all be about atoning for sin. They can stress complete consecration and purification. He quotes Block: the burnt offering was burned completely, and none of it was eaten. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/
- Keil & Delitzsch: "to slaughter on the tables" means the tables held the slaughtered meat. The killing itself happened just outside the porch. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-45.html
- Gill: the sin and guilt offerings show that Christ is a sacrifice for every kind of sin. The tables stand for the Lord's Table. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-39.html
- Bible Hub's own notes (unattributed): in the coming kingdom these sacrifices will be literal, but they will look back to Christ, much as the Lord's Supper does. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/40-39.htm

**vv. 40–41 (eight tables)**
- Keil & Delitzsch: four tables stood on each side of the porch, two inside and two against the outer wall. The same arrangement applied at all three inner gates. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-42.htm
- Benson: those who limit this to the north gate picture two tables on each side of the entrance and two on each side of the inner part. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-39.html
- Henry: the tabernacle and Solomon's temple had no such tables. These signal the "multitude of spiritual sacrifices" of the gospel age. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/40.htm

**v. 42 (four stone tables)**
- Pulpit: there were twelve tables in all, eight for slaughter and four for the tools. If the word is read as "steps" rather than "burnt offering," the tables' position changes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-39.html
- Keil & Delitzsch read the word as "steps," a staircase, and say the tables stood by the steps. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Gill (unattributed in the extract): the tables' lasting materials point to the Lord's Supper continuing until Christ returns. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-42.htm

**v. 43 (hooks)**
- Keil & Delitzsch: "double pegs, a span long," fixed around the three outer sides of the porch. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Henry: the hooks held the meat ready for the altar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/40.htm

**v. 44 (two chambers)**
- The NKJV Guzik uses says "chambers for the singers." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/
- Keil & Delitzsch: the text has "cells of singers," but vv. 45–46 make these priests' rooms. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Constable notes the Hebrew places one room beside the east inner gate, not the south one, while he follows the other reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-46.html

**v. 45 (priests in charge of the temple)**
- Barnes suggests these duties may have gone to descendants of Abiathar and Ithamar. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-46.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary reads these priests as gospel ministers who have the charge of souls. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-40.html

**v. 46 (sons of Zadok)**
- Ellicott: by the law every son of Aaron could be a priest, so limiting the altar to Zadok's line is "obscure." He suggests that so few non-Zadokite priests avoided idolatry that all faithful priests came to bear his name. On 44:15 he adds that Zadok stayed loyal in Adonijah's revolt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-45.html and https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/44-15.htm
- Benson: Zadok's family stayed true when Ithamar's line fell into idolatry. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-45.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Solomon set aside Abiathar for backing Adonijah, which fulfilled the word against Eli's house. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/ezekiel-40.html
- Barnes, Pulpit, and Keil & Delitzsch trace David's division of the priesthood between Zadok and Ahimelech (1 Chr. 24:3). They say that here only Zadokites may approach God, and Keil adds that the Ithamarites are given non-priestly work (44:10ff). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-46.htm
- Gill: Zadok means "just" and is a type of Christ. His "sons" are gospel ministers and believers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-46.htm
- Oecolampadius (in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary): "sons of Zadok" means sons of righteousness, those "justified by faith." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-40.html
- Bible Hub article: the Zadokites' exclusive access points to Christ as the only mediator. It now opens to all believers (1 Pet. 2:9). It also notes the Dead Sea Scrolls' use of "sons of Zadok." https://biblehub.com/q/Zadokites_role_in_Ezekiel_40_46.htm

**v. 47 (the square court and the altar)**
- Keil & Delitzsch: this closes the description of the courts. The altar itself is described later, in 43:13ff. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-38.htm
- Henry: no altar appears until God's glory fills the house, "for Christ is our altar." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/40.htm

**v. 48 (the temple porch)**
- Pulpit: chapter 41 should really begin here, since the house itself now starts, as in 1 Kings 6. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/40-48.htm
- Barnes: two columns plus a three-cubit opening make up five cubits on each side of a ten-cubit entrance, giving a 20-cubit front. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-49.html
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: we approach God "by slow and solemn stages," not in a rush. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-40.html
- Bible Hub's notes: the porch echoes 1 Kings 6:3. They also say this is a literal future temple. https://biblehub.com/ezekiel/40-48.htm

**v. 49 (porch size, steps, columns)**
- Barnes: Solomon's porch was 20 by 10 cubits. The extra cubit may be a space in front of the porch. The pillars were probably shafts on bases, perhaps shaped like palm trees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-49.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/ezekiel-40.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the Hebrew says eleven cubits, the Septuagint twelve. The figure of ten steps comes from the Septuagint. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-49.htm
- Poole: commentators disagree on the number of steps, but "most say eight." The pillars stood free, like Jachin and Boaz. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/40-49.htm
- Guzik and Kretzmann both compare the pillars to Jachin and Boaz. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-40.cfm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/ezekiel-40.html
- Henry: in the gospel church everything is firm and done "decently and in order." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/40.htm

---

**Where traditions differ (vv. 38–43, the sacrifices)**
The real dividing line is how to read the temple, not which denomination a teacher belongs to.
- **Literal, future sacrifices that look back as a memorial:** John MacArthur (Baptist, gty), in a Q&A on Precept Austin, says the millennial temple will have symbolic sacrifices, like the Lord's Table. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeon_on_ezekiel Guzik (Enduring Word) quotes the view that millennial sacrifices will be a memorial of Calvary, as the Lord's Supper is now. He also points to Paul taking part in temple rites in Acts 21. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/ezekiel/ezekiel-40.cfm and https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/how-many-temples-were-built-in-jerusalem-qa-with-david-guzik/
- **Spiritual, gospel-age reading:** Gill (Baptist) says the passage refers to gospel times, so legal sacrifices "are all abolished." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-38.html Matthew Henry (Presbyterian Nonconformist) reads it as spiritual sacrifices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/ezekiel/40.htm The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says going back to literal sacrifices would be a return to "beggarly elements." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/40-39.html
- **Lutheran:** Kretzmann's extract only covers the architecture, so I couldn't find his view on the sacrifices. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/ezekiel-40.html

So the Baptists in these sources fall on both sides: MacArthur reads the sacrifices as literal and future, Gill as spiritual.
